READING 39
EQUITY INSTRUMENT FEATURES
MODULE 39.1: PUBLIC AND PRIVATE EQUITY
INVESTMENTS
LOS 39.a: Describe basic features and types of equity instruments.
An equity instrument is a security that represents ownership of a portion of a
corporation. As we discussed in our Corporate Finance reading on organizational
forms, the owners of equity instruments (i.e., shareholders) can lose their
investment if a company goes bankrupt, but otherwise have no liability for
claims against the company. Equity instrument owners have a fractional claim to
a company’s assets net of any higher-priority claims, such as debts and taxes,
and may have voting rights on company policies and decisions.
Two key differences between equity instruments and debt instruments (which we
will describe in the Fixed Income topic area) are as follows:
While debt instruments have finite lives (i.e., maturities), equity instruments
have indefinite lives. An equity instrument continues to exist unless a corporate
event, such as an acquisition by another company or a liquidation of the
company, causes it to go out of existence.
Payments of interest and principal to debtholders are contractual obligations of
a company. In contrast, payments of dividends (distributions of a company’s
net income to shareholders) are at the company’s discretion.
Companies’ dividend payment policies typically change over the company life
cycle. We can think of this life cycle as having the following four phases:
Start-up phase. A start-up company initially has no revenue, and its cash flow
is negative as it spends its invested capital to establish its business. At this
stage, a company has no earnings to distribute.

Growth phase. Revenue is increasing and cash flow may change from negative
to positive, but a company is more likely to reinvest its earnings to grow the
business than distribute them to equity holders.
Mature phase. In this phase, a company has stable cash flows and may find
fewer avenues to pursue growth, so equity holders prefer that the company
distribute its earnings regularly as dividends.
Decline phase. Eventually, a company may reach a phase of decreasing
revenues and cash flows, bringing its prospects for future dividend payments
into question.
Types of Equity Instruments
Equity instruments differ in their features and legal rights. When a company
issues equity securities, it must provide potential investors an equity prospectus
that discloses these features and rights and describes how the company intends to
use the capital it will raise by selling the securities. A prospectus specifies
whether the security includes voting rights on company matters; dividend
rights to regularly scheduled or special dividends; conversion rights to change
the security to another type (e.g., from preferred shares to common shares);
liquidation rights if the company dissolves and distributes its remaining assets;
split, subdivision, or combination rights if the company splits, divides, or
combines equity shares in the future; and preemptive rights that may give the
security holder a first opportunity to buy shares the company issues in the future.
Common shares are the most frequently issued form of equity and represent an
ownership interest. Common shareholders have a residual claim (after the claims
of debtholders, other creditors, and preferred stockholders) on firm assets if the
firm is liquidated, and they govern the corporation through voting rights.
Firms are under no obligation to pay dividends on common equity; the firm
determines what dividend will be paid periodically. Common stockholders are
able to vote for the board of directors, on merger decisions, and on the selection
of auditors. If they are unable to attend the annual meeting, shareholders can
vote by proxy, having someone else vote as they direct them, on their behalf.
Common shares benefit the issuing company by allowing it to raise capital while
keeping control of its operations. Common shares benefit investors by allowing
them to acquire fractional ownership of a company while investing a small
amount relative to a company’s size.

Preference shares (or preferred stock) have features of both common stock
and debt. As with common stock, preferred stock dividends are not a contractual
obligation, and the shares usually do not mature. Like debt, preferred shares
typically make fixed periodic payments to investors and do not usually have
voting rights. Preferred shares have a stated par value and pay a percentage
dividend based on the par value of the shares. A $100 par value preferred with an
8% dividend pays a dividend of $8 per year. If the firm liquidates, preferred
shares may be entitled to a predetermined liquidation preference payout ahead
of any distributions to common shareholders.
Callable preference shares give the firm the right, but not the obligation, to
repurchase the shares at a prespecified call price. Putable preference shares
give the shareholder the right, but not the obligation, to sell the preference shares
back to the issuer at a specified price, known as the put contingency price.
Cumulative preference shares are usually promised fixed dividends, and any
dividends that are not paid must be made up before common shareholders can
receive dividends. The dividends of noncumulative preference shares do not
accumulate over time when they are not paid, but in any given period, preferred
dividends must be paid before common shareholders can receive dividends.
Investors in participating preference shares receive extra dividends if the
firm’s profits exceed a predetermined level and may receive a value greater than
the par value of the preferred stock if the firm is liquidated. Nonparticipating
preference shares have a claim equal to par value in the event of liquidation and
do not share in firm profits through extra dividends. Smaller and riskier firms
whose investors may be concerned about the firm’s future often issue
participating preferred stock so investors can share in the upside potential of the
firm.
Convertible preference shares give the preferred shareholder the right to
exchange the shares for common stock at a conversion ratio determined when
the shares are originally issued. Convertible preferred shares are often used to
finance risky early-stage firms. The conversion feature compensates investors
for the additional risk they take when investing in such firms and enables the
firms to raise capital at a lower cost than issuing common shares.
LOS 39.b: Contrast features of publicly listed versus private equity
securities.

The discussion so far has centered on equity that is publicly traded. Private
equity is usually issued to institutional investors via private placements.
Private equity has several characteristics that distinguish it from public equity.
Some of these characteristics are company-specific; some are stock-specific.
Company-specific characteristics of private equity include the following:
Typically smaller-sized companies
Earlier (start-up and growth stages) or later (decline stage) in the company life
cycle
More limited financial disclosure because private firms are not subject to the
reporting requirements that govern publicly traded firms
Greater overlap between ownership and management
More concentrated ownership
Stock-specific characteristics of private equity include the following:
Less liquidity, as no public market exists in which to trade the shares
More concentrated control of the company
Restrictions on the sale of equity shares by owners
The four main types of private equity investments are venture capital, growth
equity, buyout equity, and special situations.
Venture capital refers to the capital provided to firms early in their life cycles
to fund their start-up, development, and growth. Investors can be family,
friends, wealthy individuals, or private equity funds. Venture capital
investments are illiquid and investors often have to commit funds for several
years before they can cash out (exit) their investment.
Growth equity refers to capital a firm raises in its growth stage. Raising
additional capital at this stage can decrease the concentration of ownership that
exists at the venture capital stage.
Buyout equity tends to focus on mature-stage companies, especially when the
private equity investors believe a company is underperforming but has value
that can be realized by restructuring its capital or operations. A buyout of a
publicly traded company that results in the investing group assuming full
control is known as a take-private transaction. In a leveraged buyout (LBO),
investors buy all of a firm’s equity using debt financing (leverage). If the
buyers are the firm’s current management, the LBO is referred to as a

management buyout (MBO). Firms in LBOs usually have cash flow that is
adequate to service the issued debt or have undervalued assets that can be sold
to pay down the debt over time.
Special situations refer to private equity investment in distressed companies,
such as those in the decline stage of the life cycle, or in companies that are
restructuring or reorganizing. This may take the form of a private investment
in public equity (PIPE), in which a publicly traded firm that needs capital
quickly sells private equity to investors.
MODULE QUIZ 39.1
1. The advantage of participating preferred shares versus nonparticipating preferred shares
is that participating preferred shares can:
A. obtain voting rights.
B. receive extra dividends.
C. be converted into common stock.
2. Compared to public equity, which of the following is least likely to characterize private
equity?
A. More liquid market.
B. Lower reporting costs.
C. More concentrated ownership.
KEY CONCEPTS
LOS 39.a
An equity instrument represents ownership of a portion of a corporation.
Common shareholders have a residual claim on firm assets and govern the
corporation through voting rights. Common shares have variable dividends,
which the firm is under no legal obligation to pay.
Preferred stock typically does not mature, does not have voting rights, and has
dividends that are fixed in amount but are not a contractual obligation of the
firm.
Cumulative preferred shares require any dividends that were missed in the past
to be paid before common shareholders receive any dividends. Participating
preferred shares may receive extra dividends if firm profits exceed a prespecified
level and may receive proceeds greater than par value if the firm is liquidated.
Convertible preferred stock can be converted to common stock at a prespecified
conversion ratio.

Callable shares allow the firm the right to repurchase the shares at a prespecified
price. Putable shares give the shareholder the right to sell the shares back to the
firm at a prespecified price.
LOS 39.b
Compared to public equity, private equity has less liquidity, fewer financial
disclosures, greater overlap between ownership and management, more
concentrated ownership, and more restrictions on the sale of shares.
While public equity tends to feature mature-stage companies, private equity
investments may occur earlier or later in the company life cycle. Venture capital
is provided to firms early in their life cycles. Growth equity refers to capital a
firm raises in its growth stage. Buyout equity tends to focus on mature-stage
companies. Special situations are investments in distressed, restructuring, or
reorganizing firms.
ANSWER KEY FOR MODULE QUIZ
Module Quiz 39.1
. B Participating preferred shares can receive extra dividends if firm profits
exceed a prespecified level and a value greater than the par value if the firm
is liquidated. (LOS 39.a)
. A Private equity has less liquidity because no public market for it exists.
Ownership is typically more concentrated than a publicly traded firm.
Reporting costs are lower for private equity because the firm is not subject
to the reporting requirements that govern publicly traded firms.(LOS 39.b)
